input:
## Basis

The column has been designed to separate a liquid feed into an overhead product and a bottoms product, with the separation duty being carried by the key component. The design throughput is 24 t per day. The duty comprises a removal of 96% of the key component to the overhead product, with the remaining material leaving with the bottoms; the bottoms specification follows from the overhead recovery rather than from a separate limit. The wetted parts are manufactured from 316L stainless steel, and this grade is stated here once, being referred to in the materials section simply as the grade named in the basis. The feed is introduced as a saturated liquid at its bubble point, and the column is operated under conditions that are close to atmospheric, without vacuum, with a total condenser being provided overhead and a thermosyphon reboiler at the base. The design case is represented by the rated throughput at the stated recovery. Operation away from the design case is addressed in the risks section, where fouling and turndown are standing as open items. Design margins are held within the sizing section, in the stage allowance and in the hydraulic rating, and care has been taken to ensure that no margin is taken twice on one and the same quantity.

## Sizing

The sizing has been carried out starting from the equilibrium data for the key pair. A shortcut calculation has been used to fix the minimum stage count and the minimum reflux from the limiting conditions at total reflux and at the pinch, and the operating reflux has been set above the minimum by the margin that has been adopted for this service. The stage count is derived from the operating reflux by means of the standard stage-efficiency route, whereby the theoretical stages are converted into actual trays through the overall efficiency that is expected for the system; it should be noted that the efficiency figure represents the largest single uncertainty in the height of the column. The diameter is set by the vapour traffic at the top of the column, where the molar flow is at its greatest, rated against the flooding limit with the customary derating being applied for a foaming tendency. The tray spacing follows from the diameter and from the need for disengaging space above the liquid on each tray. The reboiler and the condenser are sized on the basis of the boil-up and condensation duties that are implied by the reflux choice, so that the three ratings — covering the stages, the diameter, and the heat transfer — are resting on one consistent set of internal flows. A hydraulic check at reduced rate is reported together with the rating, since the turndown behaviour of the trays governs the extent to which the column can be backed off before efficiency is lost; the check states the behaviour that was found, and the operating consequence is carried forward as an open item in the risks section. The pressure drop over the column is obtained by summing the tray count and the per-tray drop at the design rate, and the bottoms temperature is checked against the reboiler limit at the pressure that results.

## Materials

The grade that is named in the basis is used for every wetted part, including the shell, the trays, the downcomers, the internal supports, and the wetted faces of the nozzles. The choice is based on the corrosion behaviour of the feed and of the condensate that is formed in the overhead line, where a dilute acidic condensate is known to attack plainer grades at the first condensation surface. Welds in wetted service are made with a matching filler and are finished flush on the tray decks, where a raised bead would otherwise hold liquid and initiate a fouling site. The selection of gaskets follows the same duty: the joint faces are exposed to the full temperature swing of the column, and the gasket material is chosen for the condensate chemistry rather than for the bulk liquid. The external parts, comprising the skirt, the platforms, the insulation cladding, and the lifting attachments, are manufactured from carbon steel, are painted against the site atmosphere, and are isolated from the wetted grade at the points where the two meet, so that the joint does not become a corrosion cell. A corrosion allowance is taken on the shell courses that see the feed zone, where the liquid is at its hottest and least pure, whilst no allowance is taken on the trays, which can be replaced at a turnaround. Inspection access is provided at the feed tray and at the base, so that the condition of the internals can be judged without the need for a full entry.

## Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items, and it should be emphasised that neither of them is resolved in this report.

Fouling. The feed carries a fouling tendency that has not been measured on this material in this particular service. The design accommodates the consequences in three places: access for cleaning is provided at the feed tray and at the reboiler, a pressure-drop trend is to be watched during operation as the fouling indicator, and spare heat-transfer surface is provided in the reboiler. What is missing, however, is a fouling rate. In the absence of a rate, the cleaning interval cannot be set, and no interval is set by this report; the interval is left to be fixed from the pressure-drop trend that is observed during the first operating period. Any claim of a run length for the column would fall outside the evidence that is presently available.

Turndown. The hydraulic check that is presented in the sizing section demonstrates how the trays behave as the rate falls, although the operating limit has not yet been fixed. At low rates, the risk is represented by weeping at the trays and by a fall in stage efficiency, which acts directly on the recovery that is stated in the basis: a column that is backed off too far will no longer meet its duty, and the failure is a silent one, appearing first in the form of off-specification overhead product. The minimum operating rate, together with the control changes that are required by a low rate, are left open pending the receipt of efficiency data for the chosen tray at part load. The two items share one common feature: each of them requires operating or test data that cannot be supplied by design calculation, and each is therefore carried forward as a question for the next stage rather than being closed by assumption at this point.
